entries.topic: Documented policy levers and their evidence on both sides: 2021 CTC, minimum wage, Medicaid expansion, zoning/supply reform, baby bonds

claims.text: Ananat et al. (NBER 29823, March 2022; Columbia discussion paper Oct 2021), Census Household Pulse data April-September 2021: 'very small, inconsistently signed, and statistically insignificant' effects of the monthly expanded CTC on employment and labour-force participation of adults with children.

Corinth, Meyer, Stadnicki and Wu (NBER 29366): replacing the CTC with the 2021-style child allowance would cut child poverty about 34% (deep child poverty 39%) before behavioural effects; about 1.5 million working parents (2.6%) would leave the labour force; after that response child poverty would fall at most 22% and deep child poverty not at all. This is a projection from estimated elasticities, not observed outcomes.

CBS (12 Oct 2021): Stanford's Jacob Goldin called the key employment assumption 'really not credible'; CBPP said about 95% of recipient families had a working parent or one between jobs, ill, disabled or caring for a child under 2.

CBO (Feb 2021) on raising the federal minimum to $15 by 2025: about 1.4 million fewer workers employed (central estimate), 900,000 fewer people in poverty, net pay to affected workers +$333bn ($509bn higher wages minus $175bn lost to unemployment).

Cengiz, Dube, Lindner, Zipperer (138 state minimum-wage increases 1979-2016, bunching estimator): number of low-wage jobs essentially unchanged over five years after increases; some wage spillovers; reduced employment in tradable sectors.

Neumark and Shirley (2022): 79.2% of the preferred employment elasticities in the US literature since the early 1990s are negative; 46.2% negative and significant at 5%; for directly affected workers mean elasticity -0.270, median -0.130; evidence stronger for teens, young adults, less-educated.

Miller, Altekruse, Johnson, Wherry: ACA Medicaid expansion reduced annual mortality among low-income adults aged 55-64 by 0.132 percentage points (about 9.4% of the mean); roughly 15,600 deaths would have been averted in non-expansion states had they expanded.

Oregon Health Insurance Experiment (NEJM 2013, lottery): no statistically significant effects on blood pressure, cholesterol or HbA1c after about two years; depression down 9.2 points (30%); catastrophic out-of-pocket spending down 4.5 points (base 5.5%), nearly eliminated; borrowing/skipping bills for medical costs down 14.2 points; use and spending up about 35% (about $1,200 a year).

Bjoerkheim (Feb 2023): the mortality reduction among those uninsured before expansion (0.150 points) is only slightly larger than the full-sample effect (0.132), so the mechanism is unclear; Oregon and RAND HIE found little direct health or mortality effect.

Pew (4 Jan 2024): 2017-2022 Minneapolis housing stock +12% vs +4% rest of Minnesota; rents +1% vs +14%; about 21,000 units permitted, 87% in buildings of 20+ units, about 1% in 2-4 unit buildings; reforms: parking minimums ended citywide 2021, apartments along corridors (Minneapolis 2040), duplex/triplex on all lots (modest effect so far).

Axios (25 June 2026, on NMHC/NYU report): researchers attribute part of the slow rent growth to weaker demand after the 2020 unrest and to low interest rates fuelling construction; the slow-rent period has ended; Twin Cities rent growth fourth-fastest in the US per Yardi Matrix.

CT Baby Bonds: $3,200 invested for each child born on or after 1 July 2023 whose birth was covered by HUSKY (Medicaid); claim between ages 18 and 30 for a Connecticut home, business, education/training or retirement savings; financial-literacy course and residency required; projected $11,000-$24,000; about 15,000-16,000 eligible births a year; funded for 12 years of births.
Zewde (2018 simulation, PSID): a universal baby-bond programme would cut the young-adult white/Black median wealth ratio from about 15:1 ($45,000 vs $3,005) to about 1.6:1.

Bruenig (Jan 2019): median-based gap measures overstate baby bonds' effect; mean gap $760,700 (SCF 2016); a programme of about $80bn a year 'is not going to nearly close' a total gap over $15 trillion.

entries.topic: Additional measures used in the Dream scorecard

claims.text: NHIS 2025: 8.3% of all ages (28.0m) uninsured; adults 18-64 11.6% (13.5% in 2021); by race/ethnicity, adults 18-64: Hispanic 21.9%, Black non-Hispanic 11.3%, White non-Hispanic 8.5%, Asian non-Hispanic 4.9%; adults in non-expansion states 18.1% vs 9.0% in Medicaid expansion states.

sources.label: CDC/NCHS, 'U.S. Uninsured Rate Unchanged in 2025' (NHIS early release), 28 May 2026

claims.text: IRS (IR-2026-42, 31 Mar 2026): Trump Accounts created by the 2025 budget law (P.L. 119-21); $1,000 federal pilot contribution for US-citizen children with a valid SSN born 1 Jan 2025 to 31 Dec 2028; contributions begin 4 July 2026; more than 4 million children signed up, more than 1 million covered by pilot elections.

sources.label: Internal Revenue Service, '4 million children have been signed up for Trump Accounts with 1 million claiming the $1,000 pilot program contribution', IR-2026-42, 31 March 2026
